This Phase 3 protocol is designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of Zenziva in patients with Treatment-Resistant Depression (TRD). The primary objective is to assess the superiority of Zenziva over placebo in reducing depressive symptoms.

**Study Design**

The study will employ a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design. Patients will be randomly assigned to either the Zenziva group or the placebo group in a 1:1 ratio.

**Patient Population**

Eligible patients will be those with a diagnosis of TRD, defined as failure to respond to at least two previous antidepressant treatments. Patients will be aged 18-65 years and will have a minimum score of 25 on the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS).

**Intercurrent Events**

Intercurrent events, such as changes in concomitant medications or the occurrence of adverse events, will be carefully monitored and documented throughout the study. These events will be accounted for in the analysis using the principles of Intention-to-Treat (ITT) and Missing-at-Random (MAR) and Missing-not-at-Random (MNAR) assumptions (Rubin, 1976; Little & Rubin, 2002). To address the risk of MNAR, we will use a sensitivity analysis with a pattern mixture model (PMM) (Horton et al., 2003).

**Efficacy Endpoints**

The primary efficacy endpoint will be the change from baseline to week 8 in the MADRS total score. Secondary endpoints will include the response rate (defined as a ≥ 50% reduction in MADRS total score) and remission rate (defined as a MADRS total score ≤ 10).

**Statistical Analysis**

The statistical analysis will be performed using a Mixed-Effects Model for Repeated Measures (MMRM) (Gould, 1997), which will account for the correlation between repeated measures and provide a robust estimate of the treatment effect. The model will include the following terms:
$$

To address the risk of missing data bias, we will use a sensitivity analysis with a pattern mixture model (PMM) (Horton et al., 2003) to account for MNAR. We will also use the Multiple Imputation (MI) analysis to account for missing data (Rubin, 1987).

**Multiplicity**

To control the Family-wise Error Rate (FWER) at 0.05, we will use the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995) to adjust the p-values for multiple testing. We will also use a hierarchical testing procedure, where the primary and secondary endpoints will be tested in a pre-specified order.

The sample size calculation will be based on the primary efficacy endpoint, using a two-sample t-test with a significance level of 0.05 and a power of 90%. Assuming a standard deviation of 10 and a treatment effect of 4, the required sample size will be:

Eligible patients will be those with a diagnosis of TRD, defined as failure to respond to at least two previous antidepressant treatments. Patients will be aged 18-65 years and will have a minimum score of 25 on the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS).

$$

This Phase 3 protocol is designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of Zenziva in patients with Treatment-Resistant Depression (TRD). The primary objective is to assess the superiority of Zenziva over placebo in reducing depressive symptoms.

**Study Design**

The study will employ a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design. Patients will be randomly assigned to either the Zenziva group or the placebo group in a 1:1 ratio.

**Patient Population**

Eligible patients will be those with a diagnosis of TRD, defined as failure to respond to at least two previous antidepressant treatments. Patients will be aged 18-65 years and will have a minimum score of 25 on the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS).

**Intercurrent Events**

Intercurrent events, such as changes in concomitant medications or the occurrence of adverse events, will be carefully monitored and documented throughout the study. These events will be accounted for in the analysis using the principles of Intention-to-Treat (ITT) and Missing-at-Random (MAR) and Missing-not-at-Random (MNAR) assumptions (Rubin, 1976; Little & Rubin, 2002). To address the risk of MNAR, we will use a sensitivity analysis with a pattern mixture model (PMM) (Horton et al., 2003).

**Efficacy Endpoints**

The primary efficacy endpoint will be the change from baseline to week 8 in the MADRS total score. Secondary endpoints will include the response rate (defined as a ≥ 50% reduction in MADRS total score) and remission rate (defined as a MADRS total score ≤ 10).

**Statistical Analysis**

The statistical analysis will be performed using a Mixed-Effects Model for Repeated Measures (MMRM) (Gould, 1997), which will account for the correlation between repeated measures and provide a robust estimate of the treatment effect. The model will include the following terms:
$$
Y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{Treatment}_{ij} + \beta_2 \times \text{Visit}_{ij} + \beta_3 \times \text{Treatment}_{ij} \times \text{Visit}_{ij} + \epsilon_{ij}
$$
where $Y_{ij}$ is the MADRS total score at visit $j$ for patient $i$, $\text{Treatment}_{ij}$ is the treatment group (Zenziva or placebo), $\text{Visit}_{ij}$ is the visit number, and $\epsilon_{ij}$ is the error term.

The estimand will be defined as the difference in mean change from baseline to week 8 in MADRS total score between the Zenziva and placebo groups. This estimand is aligned with the clinical question of interest and reflects the treatment effect on the primary efficacy endpoint.

**Multiplicity**

To control the Family-wise Error Rate (FWER) at 0.05, we will use the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995) to adjust the p-values for multiple testing. We will also use a hierarchical testing procedure, where the primary and secondary endpoints will be tested in a pre-specified order.

**Introduction**

This Phase 3 protocol is designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of Zenziva in patients with Treatment-Resistant Depression (TRD). The primary objective is to assess the superiority of Zenziva over placebo in reducing depressive symptoms.

**Study Design**

The study will employ a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design. Patients will be randomly assigned to either the Zenziva group or the placebo group in a 1:1 ratio.

**Patient Population**

Eligible patients will be those with a diagnosis of TRD, defined as failure to respond to at least two previous antidepressant treatments. Patients will be aged 18-65 years and will have a minimum score of 25 on the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS).

**Intercurrent Events**

Intercurrent events, such as changes in concomitant medications or the occurrence of adverse events, will be carefully monitored and documented throughout the study. These events will be accounted for in the analysis using the principles of Intention-to-Treat (ITT) and Missing-at-Random (MAR) and Missing-not-at-Random (MNAR) assumptions (Rubin, 1976; Little & Rubin, 2002). To address the risk of MNAR, we will use a sensitivity analysis with a pattern mixture model (PMM) (Horton et al., 2003).

**Efficacy Endpoints**

The primary efficacy endpoint will be the change from baseline to week 8 in the MADRS total score. Secondary endpoints will include the response rate (defined as a ≥ 50% reduction in MADRS total score) and remission rate (defined as a MADRS total score ≤ 10).

**Statistical Analysis**

The statistical analysis will be performed using a Mixed-Effects Model for Repeated Measures (MMRM) (Gould, 1997), which will account for the correlation between repeated measures and provide a robust estimate of the treatment effect. The model will include the following terms:
$$
Y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{Treatment}_{ij} + \beta_2 \times \text{Visit}_{ij} + \beta_3 \times \text{Treatment}_{ij} \times \text{Visit}_{ij} + \epsilon_{ij}
$$
where $Y_{ij}$ is the MADRS total score at visit $j$ for patient $i$, $\text{Treatment}_{ij}$ is the treatment group (Zenziva or placebo), $\text{Visit}_{ij}$ is the visit number, and $\epsilon_{ij}$ is the error term.

**Estimand Definition**

The estimand will be defined as the difference in mean change from baseline to week 8 in MADRS total score between the Zenziva and placebo groups. This estimand is aligned with the clinical question of interest and reflects the treatment effect on the primary efficacy endpoint.

**Missing Data Bias**

To address the risk of missing data bias, we will use a sensitivity analysis with a pattern mixture model (PMM) (Horton et al., 2003) to account for MNAR. We will also use the Multiple Imputation (MI) analysis to account for missing data (Rubin, 1987).

**Multiplicity**

To control the Family-wise Error Rate (FWER) at 0.05, we will use the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995) to adjust the p-values for multiple testing. We will also use a hierarchical testing procedure, where the primary and secondary endpoints will be tested in a pre-specified order.

The sample size calculation will be based on the primary efficacy endpoint, using a two-sample t-test with a significance level of 0.05 and a power of 90%. Assuming a standard deviation of 10 and a treatment effect of 4, the required sample size will be:
$$

$$
We will recruit 150 patients per group to account for potential dropouts.

The study will be designed to provide substantial evidence to support the claims of effectiveness. The procedures used to minimize bias will be described in the protocol and report.
